This project grew out of several lines of work that were each moving toward
the same question. Here's how they came together, and where we're going next.

<p class="head-pointer"><a href="#now">Jump to where we are now <span aria-hidden="true">↓</span></a></p>

<div class="branch-legend visually-hidden">
<p>Before the project</p>
<ul aria-label="Branches before the project">
<li data-branch="error-in-science"><code>error-in-science</code> Philosophy and history of science on error, mostly in experiments</li>
<li data-branch="opacity"><code>opacity</code> Whether complex models and AI can be understood, and explainable AI</li>
<li data-branch="credibility"><code>credibility</code> Science and technology studies of how modeling communities build trust</li>
<li data-branch="ryan"><code>ryan</code> Ryan O'Loughlin's research and fieldwork</li>
<li data-branch="matt"><code>matt</code> Matthew Mayernik's research on data, documentation and credibility</li>
<li data-branch="ai-climate"><code>ai-climate</code> Climate science: model comparison, then AI weather and climate models</li>
</ul>
<p>The project</p>
<ul aria-label="Branches in the project">
<li data-branch="main"><code>main</code> The project as a whole: funding, approvals, the framework and papers</li>
<li data-branch="interviews"><code>interviews</code> Interviews and document analysis at NSF NCAR, the LEAP Center and NASA GISS</li>
<li data-branch="workshop"><code>workshop</code> The call, the two-day workshop and the people it brings together</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="git-timeline" id="how-it-started" tabindex="-1" data-fold="error-in-science opacity credibility">
<ol class="git-log">
<li class="commit" data-branch="error-in-science"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>1989</time> <span class="branch-tag">error-in-science</span></p><p class="commit-text">A philosopher sorts the errors that can creep into an experiment by the stage at which they arise. <a class="cite" href="#ref-hon-1989">Hon 1989</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ai-climate"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>1995</time> <span class="branch-tag">ai-climate</span></p><p class="commit-text">Climate scientists start running their models through the same experiments so they can be compared: CMIP, the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, still going three decades later. <a class="cite" href="#ref-meehl-2000">Meehl et al. 2000</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="error-in-science"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>1996</time> <span class="branch-tag">error-in-science</span></p><p class="commit-text">A hypothesis is well supported only if it has passed tests likely to catch errors: the idea of severe testing. <a class="cite" href="#ref-mayo-1996">Mayo 1996</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="opacity"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2004</time> <span class="branch-tag">opacity</span></p><p class="commit-text">Computer simulations are called "epistemically opaque": no person can trace every step from input to output. <a class="cite" href="#ref-humphreys-2004">Humphreys 2004</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="error-in-science"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2005</time> <span class="branch-tag">error-in-science</span></p><p class="commit-text">Nineteenth-century microscopists turned a mistake, nerve fibers damaged by handling, into a test for identifying nerve tissue. An error became a tool. <a class="cite" href="#ref-schickore-2005">Schickore 2005</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="credibility"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2007</time> <span class="branch-tag">credibility</span></p><p class="commit-text">Parts of climate models become meeting points between field scientists and modelers, binding the two groups together. <a class="cite" href="#ref-sundberg-2007">Sundberg 2007</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="error-in-science"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2008</time> <span class="branch-tag">error-in-science</span></p><p class="commit-text">Errors in computer models come from many sources: code bugs, approximations, data, and the choices built into the model itself. <a class="cite" href="#ref-parker-2008">Parker 2008</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="opacity"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2010</time> <span class="branch-tag">opacity</span></p><p class="commit-text">Skeptics argue climate models are so tangled that no success or failure can be pinned on any one part. <a class="cite" href="#ref-lenhard-2010">Lenhard and Winsberg 2010</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="error-in-science"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2012</time> <span class="branch-tag">error-in-science</span></p><p class="commit-text">Some systems don't just survive shocks and mistakes; they gain from them. Taleb calls this antifragility. <a class="cite" href="#ref-taleb-2012">Taleb 2012</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="error-in-science"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2015</time> <span class="branch-tag">error-in-science</span></p><p class="commit-text">Failure is central to how science succeeds. <a class="cite" href="#ref-firestein-2015">Firestein 2015</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="credibility"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2018</time> <span class="branch-tag">credibility</span></p><p class="commit-text">Climate modeling is a social enterprise: its knowledge is built by teams and communities, not lone modelers. <a class="cite" href="#ref-winsberg-2018">Winsberg 2018</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ryan"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2019 onward</time> <span class="branch-tag">ryan</span></p><p class="commit-text">Ryan begins interviews and site visits with climate scientists at NSF NCAR and NASA GISS.</p><p class="commit-talks">Talks: <a class="talk" href="https://www.cgd.ucar.edu/events/seminar/2022/ryan-oloughlin-132905" title="Why we should want models to disagree: the value of error diagnosis and low-skill models in climate science"><svg class="talk-icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M9 2.5h4.5V7M13.5 2.5 7.5 8.5M12 9.5V13a.5.5 0 0 1-.5.5h-8A.5.5 0 0 1 3 13V5a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5H7"/></svg>NSF NCAR, 2022</a> <a class="talk" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5XzoL6K8qBg" title="GISS Seminar, 3 May 2023"><svg class="talk-icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="8" cy="8" r="6.25"/><path class="talk-icon-fill" d="M6.5 5.4v5.2L10.6 8z"/></svg>NASA GISS, 2023<span class="visually-hidden"> (video)</span></a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="matt"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2019</time> <span class="branch-tag">matt</span></p><p class="commit-text">Matt shows that metadata and documentation are how scientists record what they know about their data and models, including known limits and errors. <a class="cite" href="#ref-mayernik-2019">Mayernik 2019</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="opacity"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2019</time> <span class="branch-tag">opacity</span></p><p class="commit-text">Explanations bolted onto AI models after training can mislead; build understandable models instead. <a class="cite" href="#ref-rudin-2019">Rudin 2019</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="credibility"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2020</time> <span class="branch-tag">credibility</span></p><p class="commit-text">CMIP shapes climate research, but what each team learns about its own model tends to stay with that team. <a class="cite" href="#ref-touze-2020">Touzé-Peiffer et al. 2020</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="matt"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2021</time> <span class="branch-tag">matt</span></p><p class="commit-text">Model comparisons earn trust by coupling institutions (rules, governance) with data infrastructure. Credibility belongs to the community, not any single model. <a class="cite" href="#ref-mayernik-2021">Mayernik 2021</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="opacity"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2022</time> <span class="branch-tag">opacity</span></p><p class="commit-text">Explainable AI arrives in climate science, but different explanation methods can disagree about the same model. Others ask what would make such explanations genuine. <a class="cite" href="#ref-mamalakis-2022">Mamalakis et al. 2022</a>; <a class="cite" href="#ref-buijsman-2022">Buijsman 2022</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ai-climate"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2022</time> <span class="branch-tag">ai-climate</span></p><p class="commit-text">FourCastNet, an AI weather model, makes fast global forecasts. <a class="cite" href="#ref-pathak-2022">Pathak et al. 2022</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ryan"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2023</time> <span class="branch-tag">ryan</span></p><p class="commit-text">Ryan shows that climate scientists can and do trace model errors to their sources, using physical reasoning, simplification and carefully varied reruns, answering the skeptics. <a class="cite" href="#ref-oloughlin-2023">O'Loughlin 2023</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ai-climate"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2023</time> <span class="branch-tag">ai-climate</span></p><p class="commit-text">FourCastNet's instability, which kept it to forecasts under ten days, is traced to math built for a flat map. Rebuilt for a sphere, it runs a year. <a class="cite" href="#ref-bonev-2023">Bonev et al. 2023</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="credibility"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2023</time> <span class="branch-tag">credibility</span></p><p class="commit-text">In applied data science work, errors become "a site of collaboration" that reveals and reshapes how people work together. <a class="cite" href="#ref-lin-2023">Lin and Jackson 2023</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="opacity"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2024</time> <span class="branch-tag">opacity</span></p><p class="commit-text">Climate scientists publish guides for choosing among explainable-AI methods, a sign of how widely they're now used. <a class="cite" href="#ref-bommer-2024">Bommer et al. 2024</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ryan"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2025</time> <span class="branch-tag">ryan</span></p><p class="commit-text">Ryan and coauthors urge AI climate research to look beyond after-the-fact explanations, toward knowing which part of a model does what. <a class="cite" href="#ref-oloughlin-2025">O'Loughlin et al. 2025</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ai-climate"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>February 2025</time> <span class="branch-tag">ai-climate</span></p><p class="commit-text">An AI forecast model goes into operational use at ECMWF, Europe's weather center, alongside its physics-based one. <a class="cite" href="#ref-ecmwf-2025">ECMWF 2025</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="credibility"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2025</time> <span class="branch-tag">credibility</span></p><p class="commit-text">Climate model developers describe debugging that resists standard procedures, aiming for models that are "good enough". <a class="cite" href="#ref-proske-2025">Proske and Melsen 2025</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ryan"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>August 2025</time> <span class="branch-tag">ryan</span></p><p class="commit-text">Pilot interviews at NSF NCAR. A first finding: scientists often avoid the word "error", preferring "bias", "limitation" or "statistical distinguishability". <a class="cite" href="#ref-parker-2008">Parker 2008</a> as the starting typology</p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="ryan"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>In progress</time> <span class="branch-tag">ryan</span></p><p class="commit-text">Ryan identifies four kinds of antifragility in modeling: flexibility, new hypotheses, learning from error signals, and credibility won by overcoming failure. <a class="cite" href="#ref-oloughlin-ms">O'Loughlin, manuscript</a></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="error-in-science"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2026</time> <span class="branch-tag">error-in-science</span></p><p class="commit-text">Allchin argues for "negative knowledge": knowing about errors, and how they were corrected, is knowledge too. <a class="cite" href="#ref-allchin-2026">Allchin 2026</a></p></li>
<li class="commit merge" data-branch="main"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2026</time> <span class="branch-tag">merge into main</span></p><p class="commit-text"><strong>These lines of work were all moving toward one question none had asked directly: how can errors, and the ways scientists handle them, make AI-driven science better?</strong></p></li>
<li class="commit" data-branch="main"><span class="commit-dot" aria-hidden="true"></span><p class="commit-meta"><time>2026</time> <span class="branch-tag">main</span></p><p class="commit-text">The team forms: Ryan O'Loughlin (philosophy of climate modeling, Queens College, CUNY) and Matthew Mayernik (data and credibility, NSF NCAR), with an <a href="people.qmd">advisory board</a> of philosophers, STS scholars and scientists.</p></li>

## The questions

::: {.project-links}
::: {.project-card}
### Understanding

When scientists diagnose why an AI model failed, what do they come to
understand about the model, and what does that mean for explainable AI?
:::

::: {.project-card}
### Antifragility

When do errors leave models and research communities stronger, not just
repaired, and better off than immediate success would have?
:::

::: {.project-card}
### Credibility

How do the ways teams diagnose, document and share errors build or erode trust
in the science and data they produce?
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Proposal wording

1. How do errors in AI-driven models contribute to or constrain scientific
   understanding, and what do practices of error diagnosis reveal about model
   explainability?
2. In what ways do modeling communities develop antifragile responses to error,
   using failures to strengthen rather than merely repair their systems?
3. How do errors and their management shape the credibility of AI-driven models
   and the social organization of modeling teams?
:::

## How we work

::: {.method-grid}
::: {.project-card}
### Interviews

20 or more people at each of NSF NCAR, the LEAP Center and NASA GISS:
scientists, software engineers and data specialists.
:::

::: {.project-card}
### Documents

Reports, papers, code repositories, issue trackers and dataset records, to see
how errors get written down, or don't.
:::

::: {.project-card}
### Analysis

Bringing what we hear into conversation with philosophy of science and STS, to
say when errors help science.
:::

::: {.project-card}
### Workshop

Two days for philosophers, STS scholars and scientists to test the framework.
:::
:::
